items.title: Specifying drinking fountains for GCC schools: what to put in the tender
items.excerpt: A school fountain in the Gulf has to cope with heat, salt air and heavy daily use. Here is what I would write into the specification so the units you approve are the right ones for the site.
items.cover_alt: Two pupils drinking from stainless steel pedestal fountains under a shade canopy in a school courtyard
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
A drinking fountain looks like the simplest line on a school BOQ, but the problems that show up later are usually written in at specification stage. Warm water, blocked bubblers and units that cannot take the sun all start with what went into the tender.

I have spent about 30 years in industrial equipment sales, so here is what I would put in the tender for a [school in the GCC](https://aquelon.com/sectors/education/).

## Start with the number of units, not the model

Decide how many outlets the site needs before anyone picks a product. Table 403.1 of the International Plumbing Code is a useful starting point. [The 2021 edition of the table](https://codes.iccsafe.org/s/IPC2021P1/chapter-4-fixtures-faucets-and-fixture-fittings/IPC2021P1-Ch04-Sec403.1) sets one drinking fountain per 100 occupants for educational facilities. Check what your authority actually adopts, because it varies by emirate and by country.

Then think about where pupils are, not just how many. Break times bring large numbers of pupils into the same place at once, and outlets grouped at the far end of a corridor can meet the ratio and still leave a queue. Put outlets where the crowds form: playgrounds, sports halls, canteens and the main circulation routes.

## Write the climate into the specification

A unit that performs well in a mild climate is not automatically fit for a Riyadh playground in August, so write the site conditions into the specification.

- **Chilled water where pupils actually drink.** Outdoor pipework in direct sun heats the water standing in it, and warm water is less inviting to drink. Specify a chiller or a [chilled bottle filler](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-mgym74-a021/) for the main outlets, and confirm shade and a power supply before you approve it. For that unit the guidance is to install it beneath an overhang away from direct sunlight, and continual ambient temperatures above 80°F (about 27°C) may wear the compressor prematurely. Ask for the same guidance on any chilled unit you are offered.
- **Stainless steel grade.** Near the sea, consider AISI 316 rather than 304. It has [better resistance to pitting in chloride environments](https://www.assda.asn.au/stainless-steel/grade-selection/316-the-first-step-up). If you prefer a powder coated finish, ask the manufacturer what coastal exposure it is warranted for.
- **Powder coat to a RAL reference.** If the architect wants colour, write the RAL number into the spec and ask for a physical sample before approval. Screen colours lie.

## Design for heavy use and abuse

Schools are hard on equipment, so write robustness into the specification.

- Vandal resistant bubblers with a protective guard, so mouths never touch the outlet.
- Push buttons that are mechanical and self closing, or sensor operation if the budget allows. Avoid twist taps.
- Fixings that cannot be undone with a coin or a ruler.
- Units bolted to a proper base or wall, not just sealed to the floor.

## Make it accessible

Specify at least one accessible outlet at every location. A [dual height unit](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-grm45/) gives a lower bowl for wheelchair users and younger pupils and a standard height bowl for older pupils and staff. Check the lower bowl height against your youngest age group. Ask for the clear knee space and the reach range to be shown on the datasheet. [Section 602 of the ADA Standards](https://www.access-board.gov/ada/#ada-602) is a useful benchmark. It covers knee and toe clearance, operable parts and spout height.

## Put bottle fillers in the mix

If pupils carry reusable bottles, a bottle filling station handles that better than a bubbler, and [some units have a bottle counter display](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-bf16s/).

A [combination unit](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-gym74/) puts a bubbler and a bottle filler on one pedestal, so you get both in one unit.

## Plan the water quality

A fountain is only as good as what comes into it. Specify an inline filter at each unit, sized for the expected flow, and put filter changes on the maintenance schedule from day one. Write in who changes them and how often. If nobody owns the filter, nobody changes it.

## What the submittal pack should include

Ask every bidder for the same pack so you compare like with like:

- Product datasheet with dimensions, flow rates, materials and connections
- CE declaration of conformity and the manufacturer's quality management certificate
- Hygiene or drinking water approval for the materials in contact with water
- Installation guide with the fixing and plumbing details
- Warranty terms and the local service arrangement
- Lead time to site, by model

If a bidder cannot produce these quickly, that tells you something about the support you will get in year three. Our [technical library](https://aquelon.com/library/) holds catalogues, certifications and our warranty policy, with installation guides on request.

## The short version

Count outlets by where pupils gather. Chill the water. Match the steel to the site. Specify for abuse. Make every location accessible. Put bottle fillers in the mix. Own the filters.

Get those right in the tender and the fountains stop being the line that bites you.

If you are writing a school specification now, [send me the scope](https://aquelon.com/quote/). We will come back with a priced quote within one working day.

## Sources

- International Code Council, "2021 International Plumbing Code, Table 403.1 Minimum Number of Required Plumbing Fixtures", 2021. https://codes.iccsafe.org/s/IPC2021P1/chapter-4-fixtures-faucets-and-fixture-fittings/IPC2021P1-Ch04-Sec403.1
- US Access Board, "ADA Accessibility Standards, section 602 Drinking Fountains". https://www.access-board.gov/ada/#ada-602
- Australian Stainless Steel Development Association, "316: The First Step Up". https://www.assda.asn.au/stainless-steel/grade-selection/316-the-first-step-up

items.title: Counting the bottles: what a refill station actually saves
items.excerpt: On these planning assumptions, a refill programme for 600 people replaces 150,000 plastic bottles a year. Here is the arithmetic, the estimates behind it, and how to adapt them to your own site.
items.cover_alt: A stainless steel drinking fountain beside a running track in a Gulf city park at sunset
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
Refill stations are one of the easier places to put a number on a sustainability goal. The sum is simple, and you can test every assumption behind it.

Here is the arithmetic, with the assumptions on the table.

## The basic sum

Bottles avoided in a year is people on site, times refills per person per day, times days the site is open.

Take an office with 600 people, each refilling once a day, open on weekdays only, about 250 days a year. A school will have fewer open days, so use its own calendar.

600 × 1 × 250 = **150,000 bottles a year.**

That assumes everyone takes part and every refill replaces one bought 500 ml bottle. Lower take up gives a lower number, so adjust it for your site.

## Turning bottles into plastic, carbon and money

These are the planning assumptions we use in the [calculator on our homepage](https://aquelon.com/#impact). They are estimates, not certified figures, and you should swap in your own if you have them.

| Assumption | Value we use |
| --- | --- |
| PET in a 500 ml bottle | 10 g |
| Carbon per bottle, production to disposal | 80 g CO₂e |
| Price per bottle | AED 1.00 |

On 150,000 bottles that comes to:

- **1.5 tonnes** of PET plastic that never gets made, shipped or thrown away
- **12 tonnes** of CO₂e avoided
- **AED 150,000** of bottled water spend replaced

These are gross figures. They make no allowance for the electricity, water or equipment the refill station itself uses.

Double the refills to two a day and every number doubles. Open seven days a week, as a hospital, airport or mall does, and multiply by 365 instead of 250.

## Why this matters for reporting

[LEED](https://www.usgbc.org/leed) covers water use, materials and waste, and Abu Dhabi's [Estidama Pearl Rating System](https://www.dmt.gov.ae/en/adm/Media-Centre/News/08Jan2025) assesses buildings against sustainability requirements. Neither scheme is a reason to assume a refill programme earns credit. What it gives you is a number to put against goals on water, materials and waste, so check which credits or targets your project is actually going for.

Two things make the number stronger.

**Measure it.** [Some bottle filling stations](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-bf16s/) have an optional bottle counter display. A counter replaces the refill assumption with actual use. The plastic, carbon and cost figures remain estimates.

**Make it easy.** Usage follows convenience. Put refill stations where people already walk, chill the water, and make sure there is no queue. A unit tucked behind a stairwell does not move the number.

## Where the savings are biggest

The sites with the most people per day win: [airports and metro stations](https://aquelon.com/sectors/airports-transit/), [universities and large schools](https://aquelon.com/sectors/education/), [hospitals](https://aquelon.com/sectors/healthcare/) and [stadiums](https://aquelon.com/sectors/sports-leisure/). For a stadium, work the sum per event as well as per year.

## Run your own numbers

Our [impact calculator](https://aquelon.com/#impact) does this sum for sites of 50 to 5,000 people in a few seconds and shows the assumptions underneath it. Put in your head count, refills and opening days, and use the result in your business case.

If you want help sizing a refill programme for a specific site, [send the floor plan and the occupancy](https://aquelon.com/quote/). We will come back with a priced quote within one working day.

## Sources

- US Green Building Council, "LEED rating system". https://www.usgbc.org/leed
- Abu Dhabi City Municipality, "Abu Dhabi City Municipality Promotes Sustainable Green Building Concept and Projects", 8 January 2025. https://www.dmt.gov.ae/en/adm/Media-Centre/News/08Jan2025

items.title: ANSI Z358.1 in plain English: the eyewash and shower checks that fail audits
items.excerpt: A unit that met the standard on the day it was installed can still fail an audit later. Here are five common reasons, with the numbers that matter.
items.cover_alt: A green combination safety shower and eyewash station on a grated floor in a process plant
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
I grew Hughes Safety Showers from £3.9M to £6.9M, and I built Z358 One to record eyewash and shower inspections. A unit that met the standard on the day it went in can still fail later. Here are five common ways that happens.

[ANSI/ISEA Z358.1](https://safetyequipment.org/worker_protections/emergency-eyewash-shower/) is the American national standard for emergency eyewash and shower equipment. EN 15154 is the European series, with parts including [laboratory body showers](https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-1-2025) and [plumbed in eyewash units](https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-2-2025), so check which part your project names. This is the plain English version of what the American standard asks for, and where sites fall down. The equipment itself sits in our [Emergency division](https://aquelon.com/divisions/emergency/).

## The numbers that matter

The full standard is a paid document from its publisher. These figures come from [Bradley's quick compliance guide to Z358.1](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149), which gives the section number for each, with the temperature range from [ANSI's own summary](https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/ansi-z358-1-emergency-eyewash-station-shower/) and the annual check from [Bradley's guide to the standard](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf).

| Requirement | What Z358.1 asks for |
| --- | --- |
| Reach | Within 10 seconds of the hazard, with 16.8 metres as the guideline, on the same level |
| Activation | Valve opens in one second or less and stays open until closed by hand |
| Eyewash flow | At least 1.5 litres per minute for a full 15 minutes |
| Eye and face wash flow | At least 11 litres per minute for a full 15 minutes |
| Shower flow | At least 76 litres per minute for a full 15 minutes |
| Water temperature | Tepid, about 16°C to 38°C |
| Shower head height | Between 208 cm and 244 cm above the floor |
| Spray pattern | At least 50.8 cm across at 152 cm above the floor |
| Weekly check | Activate every plumbed unit to clear the line and confirm flow |
| Annual check | Inspect every unit each year to confirm it complies |

Those numbers are the easy part. Keeping a site inside them is the hard part.

## Fail one: the water is too hot

Heat is the obvious risk in the Gulf. [The standard says tepid](https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/ansi-z358-1-emergency-eyewash-station-shower/), with 16 to 38°C as the range. An exposed supply line in summer can take the first minutes of flow above that, and [Bradley's guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) notes that environmental conditions often require freeze or scald protection. Tepid is there for a reason: [the same guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) says it is to encourage the injured person to keep flushing for the full 15 minutes.

The fix is designed in, not bolted on. Specify a tempered water system sized for the full flow: a chiller or a [tank shower with a chiller option](https://aquelon.com/products/hughes-exp-j-14ks-1500/). A [thermostatic mixing valve](https://aquelon.com/products/acorn-et71-1-bvs-otg/) can suit eyewash flows, but check its rated flow against the unit, and remember it can only blend the water it is given. Insulate and shade the supply line. Then test the temperature at the outlet in July, not in January.

## Fail two: something is in the way

The route to the unit has to be clear and on the same level. Ten seconds is not long. A pallet, a hose reel or a new piece of plant parked in front of the shower breaks that, and so can a door added after commissioning. [A door counts as an obstruction](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149). The one exception is a single unlocked door that opens in the direction of travel, and only where the contaminant is not hazardous or corrosive.

Walk the route from each hazard, time it, and repeat it every time the layout changes.

## Fail three: nobody runs it weekly

The weekly activation of a plumbed unit does two jobs. It proves nothing is blocking the flow, and it clears the stagnant water sitting in the pipe, which [Bradley's guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) names as a contamination risk. That standing water is what the injured worker gets first.

[Self contained units do not need activating, but they do need a visual inspection](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf).

Give every unit a named owner, and log the check. [Z358 One](https://z358one.com/) exists for that job: weekly activations and annual inspections are timestamped and stored in a compliance record, instead of living on a clipboard.

## Fail four: flow is below the minimum

Pressure drops as a site grows. A shower that delivered 76 litres per minute at commissioning can fall below the line once new users are added to the same main. Eyewash nozzles also scale up and partially block, especially with hard water.

Measure it properly. For eyewash units, [Bradley's guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) calls for a flow meter for the flow rate and a test gauge for the spray pattern. For showers, [its guide to the standard](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) describes a drench shower tester with a bucket to contain the water and measure it against the 20 US gallons per minute minimum. Do not eyeball it. Protect eyewash heads from contaminants and keep the nozzles clean.

## Fail five: you cannot see it

The standard calls for a [highly visible sign close to the unit and adequate lighting around it](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf). Signs fade in UV, get painted over during shutdowns and get hidden by new cabling. A worker with chemicals in their eyes is not reading small print. Check the signage and lighting at every annual inspection.

## What to put in the specification

If you are writing a spec for a new facility, ask for:

- Units independently evaluated by a third party against the standard your project names, ANSI Z358.1 or the relevant part of EN 15154
- A tempered water solution sized for 15 minutes of full flow at peak summer supply temperature
- Scald protection for the heat, and freeze protection only where it is genuinely needed
- Stainless or coated finishes suited to the chemicals on site
- Flow and temperature test results at commissioning, recorded per unit
- Data sheets and certificates for the submittal pack
- A weekly and annual inspection regime handed over with the equipment

## The short version

Compliant on day one is not the same as compliant on audit day. Control the temperature. Keep the route clear. Run every plumbed unit every week. Measure flow once a year. Make sure people can see it.

If you are specifying or replacing emergency equipment, [send the layout and the hazard list](https://aquelon.com/quote/). We will come back with a priced quote within one working day.

## Sources

- International Safety Equipment Association, "American National Standard for Emergency Eyewash and Shower Equipment", ANSI/ISEA Z358.1-2014 (R2020). https://safetyequipment.org/worker_protections/emergency-eyewash-shower/
- Bradley Corporation, "ANSI/ISEA Z358.1-2014 Quick Compliance Guide". https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149
- Bradley Corporation, "A Guide to the ANSI/ISEA Z358.1-2014 Standard for Emergency Eyewashes and Shower Equipment". https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf
- American National Standards Institute, "ANSI Z358.1-2014: Emergency Eyewash and Shower Standard". https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/ansi-z358-1-emergency-eyewash-station-shower/
- Estonian Centre for Standardisation, "EVS-EN 15154-1:2025, Plumbed-in body showers for laboratories", 2025. https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-1-2025
- Estonian Centre for Standardisation, "EVS-EN 15154-2:2025, Plumbed-in eyewash units", 2025. https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-2-2025
